summary:
## Background
Clopidogrel requires CYP2C19-mediated bioactivation. Loss‑of‑function (LOF) CYP2C19 alleles can blunt antiplatelet effect and worsen outcomes. This prospective, multicenter, nonrandomized trial in South Korea (n=2910 acute ischemic stroke patients) examined whether CYP2C19 genotype modifies clinical outcomes on clopidogrel. Genotypes assayed were CYP2C19*1, *2, *3, and *17; patients were grouped as LOF carriers (any *2 or *3: intermediate or poor metabolizers) versus noncarriers (extensive metabolizers: *1/*1, *1/*17, *17/*17). Clopidogrel was maintained (aspirin co-therapy allowed).

## Key Findings
- LOF carriers had a higher 6‑month risk of composite cardiovascular events (recurrent stroke, MI, cardiovascular death) than noncarriers: 2.7% (49/1785) vs 1.6% (18/1125); HR for noncarriers vs carriers 0.58 (95% CI 0.34–1.00); log-rank P=0.048; adjusted HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.33–0.99; P=0.049).
- Recurrent stroke drove the difference: 2.5% vs 1.4%; HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.32–1.00); P=0.047. MI and cardiovascular death were rare and not different between groups.
- Safety did not differ by genotype: major bleeding 0.6% vs 0.8% (P=0.56); all‑cause mortality 0.3% vs 0.1% (P=0.27).
- Within LOF carriers, intermediate vs poor metabolizers had similar risk (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.49–1.88; P=0.92). An exploratory subgroup suggested greater benefit of noncarrier status among smokers (HR 0.09; 95% CI 0.01–0.64; P=0.02; interaction P=0.03).
- Variant interpretation: LOF alleles were CYP2C19*2 and *3 (risk of events increased on clopidogrel); noncarrier status included CYP2C19*1/*1 and gain‑of‑function–containing genotypes without LOF (e.g., *1/*17, *17/*17) and was associated with lower event risk.

## Clinical Implications
- CYP2C19 LOF alleles (*2, *3) identify stroke patients at higher risk of recurrent vascular events on clopidogrel, without a parallel increase in major bleeding. Noncarrier genotypes (*1/*1, *1/*17, *17/*17) have better outcomes on clopidogrel.
- Genotype‑guided antiplatelet selection should be considered, particularly in populations with high LOF prevalence (e.g., East Asians). For LOF carriers, alternatives not dependent on CYP2C19 activation (e.g., ticagrelor) may provide more reliable protection, consistent with prior randomized data.
- Practical notes: This was a nonrandomized study with 6‑month follow‑up and conducted in Korean centers; nonetheless, results align with the pharmacology of clopidogrel and prior literature, supporting early CYP2C19 testing to personalize secondary stroke prevention.
